about.title: Porterville Slip & Fall & Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Falls happen fast — a wet floor at a market on Olive Avenue, a broken step near Main Street, uneven pavement outside a business on Morton Avenue. What happens next often matters more than the fall itself. Under California law, a property owner isn't automatically responsible just because someone got hurt on their land; the injured person generally has to show the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn people about it. That's why documenting the scene, getting names of witnesses, and asking the property to preserve any surveillance footage can matter so much in the days that follow. Our team handles premises liability claims in Porterville and can look at the specifics of what happened and explain your options. We work on a contingency basis, meaning there's no fee unless you recover.

whyChoose.title: Why the Right Details Matter in a Porterville Fall Case

items.title: Notice Is Everything
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard before your fall. We can help gather maintenance logs, prior complaints, or incident reports that speak to that notice.

items.title: Surveillance Footage Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many Porterville businesses overwrite security video within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request preservation of that footage can be the difference between having evidence and having none.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, a Claim
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you're found partly responsible for the fall, that doesn't bar you from pursuing compensation — it may just adjust the amount.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Porterville?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a premises liability lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a government entity — such as a city building or public sidewalk — the deadline is much shorter and requires an early claim, so it's worth getting advice quickly.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for my fall?
items.answer: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, being partly responsible doesn't stop you from seeking compensation. Instead, any amount recovered would typically be reduced by your percentage of fault, so it's still worth having a case reviewed.

items.question: Do I need to prove the property owner knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Yes, in most cases you'll need to show the owner knew or reasonably should have known about the dangerous condition and failed to address it. This is why documenting things like spill duration, lighting, or prior complaints about a hazard on corridors like Henderson Avenue or Main Street can strengthen a claim.

items.question: Do you charge anything to review my case?
items.answer: No, our initial case review is completely free. We work on contingency, meaning we only get paid if you recover compensation.
